thread.title: Spotify has fans on Wall Street as it prepares to go public - MarketWatch

author: Emily Bary
title: Spotify has fans on Wall Street as it prepares to go public - MarketWatch

organizations.name: marketwatch shares of spotify technology inc.

text:
Shares of Spotify Technology Inc. have yet to begin trading, but analysts already like the sound of the streaming-music company.
At least three analysts have initiated coverage of Spotify SPOT, +0.00% shares with the equivalent of buy ratings ahead of the expected trading debut on Tuesday. It’s unusual for analysts, particularly at big firms, to publish recommendations on stocks before trading begins due to quiet periods imposed on underwriting firms. But because Spotify is forgoing a traditional initial public offering in favor of a direct listing, the company isn’t raising money from Wall Street, so analysts are free to comment away.
Don’t miss: 5 things to know about Spotify’s direct listing
RBC Capital Markets analyst Mark Mahaney is the biggest Spotify bull so far, with an overweight rating and a $220 price target, “representing 70%+ upside vs. recent private transaction price of $127.50.” He likes Spotify’s standing as the leading subscription streaming service and thinks the company can withstand competition from tech giants like Apple Inc. AAPL, -0.66% and Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, -5.21%
“We see several factors that should help Spotify maintain its leadership,” he wrote, including a strong brand and a “platform-neutral presence.”
Spotify has the top music app on Android and Apple phones in at least half of the top 20 markets, not including China, he said. Mahaney also points to Spotify’s well-received personalization efforts and the variety brought about by its paid and free tiers.
See also: Three ways Apple could spend $163 billion besides a big acquisition
Mahaney sees room for Spotify to expand its gross margin as it continues to secure better terms with the labels and benefits from the further scaling of its ad business. Spotify’s gross margin rose to 21% last year from 14% a year earlier, and the company is targeting margins of 30% to 35% for the long term.
MKM Partners analyst Rob Sanderson also predicts “a much larger margin opportunity” for Spotify, though he thinks that margin expansion won’t necessary come “at the expense of music label profits.” Sanderson is intrigued by the fact that more than 30% of streams are programmed, rather than directly requested.
“We expect Spotify will increasingly work with labels to promote artists and that labels will excuse royalty obligations from promotional content,” Sanderson wrote. “This can be considered marketing expense by labels, which typically allocate 15% to 20% of revenue to marketing functions.”
He reminds investors that because of Spotify’s unconventional choice of a direct listing, there’s a lot that investors don’t know heading into trading, including what supply will be like. The uncertainty is exacerbated by recent struggles for the S&P 500 SPX, -2.23% and tech-heavy Nasdaq COMP, -2.74% indexes.
“We are anticipating unusual trading dynamics in the days and weeks following the April 3 listing and are unsure how long before adequate liquidity will be established,” wrote Sanderson, who has a $200 price target and a buy rating on the stock. “Our target is a 12-month view independent of potential supply/demand irregularities on low trading volume immediately following the listing.”
Related: IPO proceeds hit 3-year high in first quarter, fueled by foreign offerings
James Cordwell of Atlantic Equities is also upbeat on the stock, beginning coverage with an overweight rating and a $160 year-end price target. Cordwell points out that Spotify’s average revenue per user, or ARPU, has been falling as more users pack onto family plans, which has shifted the company’s business model more toward a “per household” one.
That said, he notes that Spotify has been able to post strong revenue growth even amid the declines in ARPU, which he expects to become less significant “as the pace of the mix shift to family plans moderates.”
Cordwell echoed the optimism about margin-expansion potential, writing that he models Spotify turning profitable in 2020 while generating a 28.3% gross margin.
